module_title: Amazon S3 Object Storage, Security and Lifecycle Architecture
review_basis: Individually visually reviewed SAP Module 09 original WebP slides 4–6 including each panel, diagram, arrows and decision notes.
part_title: Private S3 Access, Encryption and Version Recovery

scenes.title: S3 access points, gateway endpoints and endpoint policies
scenes.visual_overview: This original slide explains s3 access points, gateway endpoints and endpoint policies through the pictured architecture panels, boundaries and examples.
visual_walkthrough: Follow several applications through a named S3 access point with scoped policy while retaining bucket authorization
Contrast VPC gateway endpoint route-table integration with S3 interface endpoints and their network costs
Distinguish a private network path or endpoint policy from the permission needed to read a specific object
scenes.visual_example: An EC2 workload uses an S3 gateway endpoint, but the endpoint policy permits one bucket only and the bucket policy must separately authorize its IAM role.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A private route is not the same as authorization.
scenes.narration: This slide separates three controls. On the left, named S3 access points give applications appropriately scoped entry points and policies, but the underlying bucket must also authorize the operation. In the center, supported VPC traffic reaches S3 through a gateway endpoint that integrates with selected route tables; interface endpoints meet different access requirements and carry distinct costs. On the right, a policy and shield show defense in depth: the endpoint policy filters requests through the endpoint but does not grant bucket access or encrypt data by itself. For a private EC2 application, verify its route, endpoint policy, bucket policy and role permissions separately. A private route is not the same as authorization.

scenes.title: S3 encryption at rest, KMS access and HTTPS transport
scenes.visual_overview: This original slide explains s3 encryption at rest, kms access and https transport through the pictured architecture panels, boundaries and examples.
visual_walkthrough: Start at the encrypted object: explain SSE-S3 versus SSE-KMS key-management and audit responsibilities
Follow the key on the right: evaluate IAM permissions, KMS key policy and regional key availability for encrypted object operations
Use the HTTPS panel to explain transport protection and plan access for readers, replication and disaster recovery
scenes.visual_example: A replicated object is inaccessible to a recovery role because the object policy is correct but the destination KMS key policy does not authorize decrypt.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Strong encryption that blocks your recovery team is an operational failure.
scenes.narration: The central chained object represents encryption at rest, but the meaningful architecture decision is who can operate the key. SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS protect stored objects with different key-management, authorization and audit characteristics. In the right pane, S3 permission alone may be insufficient when an object uses a customer-managed KMS key. Check the IAM role, key policy and required key operations in the correct Region. The lower pane then adds HTTPS transport and policy conditions that reject insecure requests when appropriate. Design for every legitimate reader, cross-account replication and disaster recovery, not merely the upload principal. Strong encryption that blocks your recovery team is an operational failure.

scenes.title: S3 versioning, delete markers and lifecycle cost
scenes.visual_overview: This original slide explains s3 versioning, delete markers and lifecycle cost through the pictured architecture panels, boundaries and examples.
visual_walkthrough: Follow successive overwrites creating distinct object versions under one key
Distinguish a delete marker from permanent deletion of a specific version; explain recovery choices
Inspect noncurrent-version lifecycle policies and clarify that suspending versioning does not remove old versions
scenes.visual_example: An operator accidentally deletes a production configuration object. A delete marker may conceal the current object while an earlier version is recoverable; deleting a specific version is different.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Versioning enables recovery options, but lifecycle, retention and permissions determine what remains usable.
scenes.narration: On the left, observe the file stack accumulating versions each time the key is overwritten. When versioning is enabled, a delete without a version ID commonly creates a delete marker rather than erasing every stored version. On the upper-right, recovery requires selecting the correct object version or addressing the applicable delete marker. An explicit deletion of a particular version can remove that version permanently unless retention protection prevents it. The lower-right illustrates growing storage charges from noncurrent versions and markers. Configure lifecycle transitions and expiration with recovery goals in mind. Suspending versioning changes future behavior; it does not automatically clean existing history. Versioning enables recovery options, but lifecycle, retention and permissions determine what remains usable.
